query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a Si‐based silicide coating (using a Si-20Cr-20Fe fused slurry method) to a refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaTiW) will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a continuous protective silicide/oxide layer, thereby reducing oxidation rates compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (such as MoNbTaTiW) in its as-cast or uncoated state, which is susceptible to oxidation at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating via a fused slurry method to the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (e.g., air) at extreme temperatures (around 1000°C) for a prolonged period (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a double-layer coating structure: an outer high-silicon content layer (predominantly MSi2) and an inner lower-silicon content layer (mainly M5Si3), which together evolve into a protective silicide/oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the silicide coating undergoes oxidation, wherein the silicon promotes the formation of a slow-growing, adherent oxide scale that hinders further oxygen diffusion into the substrate, thus mitigating oxidation-induced degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated refractory high-entropy alloy will exhibit significantly lower mass gain due to oxidation, reduced oxide scale spallation, and enhanced structural integrity relative to the uncoated sample under the same high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory HEA typically develops a thick, non-protective oxide scale with considerable spallation and rapid oxygen ingress under high-temperature conditions, leading to accelerated degradation.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness may depend on coating uniformity, thickness, and the alloy’s composition; the protective behavior is expected specifically under high-temperature (around 1000°C) and prolonged oxidizing conditions. Extrapolation to other refractory HEAs or lower temperature regimes may require further validation.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance is uncertain and may vary with processing parameters, coating adhesion, and microstructural variations. Further experimental optimization is required to determine the precise performance gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MoNbTaTiW refractory HEA samples: one set with the applied Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating using the fused slurry method, and one uncoated control group. Expose both sets to an air atmosphere at 1000°C for 100 hours. Post-exposure, perform mass gain measurements, microstructural analyses (using SEM/EDS and XRD), and adhesion tests of the oxide scale.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (mg/cm²) to quantify oxidation kinetics
Microstructural characterization of the oxide/silicide layers
Adhesion quality and spallation assessment of the coating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in mass gain, spallation, and degradation compared to the uncoated control (or if the protective silicide/oxide layer is absent or non-adherent based on microstructural analyses), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature.
